blocks.text: …expanding the comfort zone
Definition and purpose 🐕
Scouting techniques are trained, advanced skills of the dog owner and the dog in the areas of perception techniques, movement techniques, meditation techniques and reaction techniques.
They give us comprehensive advantages in confidently leading our dog in a social environment and serve as advanced conflict prevention.
Scouting techniques bring us and our dog into harmony with the respective environmental conditions. We are able to respond appropriately to a wide range of influences and to act optimally as a team.
Prerequisites are: continuous training of the “DOWN” command and an already well-trained TEAM WALK.
Scouting techniques are trained, advanced skills of the dog owner and the dog in the areas of perception techniques, movement techniques, meditation techniques and reaction techniques.
They give us comprehensive advantages in confidently leading our dog in a social environment and serve as advanced conflict prevention.
Prerequisites: continuous training of the “DOWN” command and an already well-trained TEAM WALK.
Basics and preparation 👃
At first, we train in quiet, remote terrain without disruptive distraction. We should already have been out with the dog for a while beforehand, so that he has had some exercise.

As learned in the TEAM WALK, we move calmly through the terrain. We watch our dog attentively and notice when he reacts conspicuously with his nose to a distant stimulus. We recognise this by an increasing breathing rate with the head raised at the same time, which indicates heightened analysis of the incoming scents. This is often underlined by the mouth being held slightly open.

We need to know that our dog, with an olfactory mucosa surface 25 times larger and a scent sensitivity up to 1 million times greater for certain substances, is insurmountably superior to us humans, and that, by means of a special palatal organ, he is also able to convert scents into taste.
Procedure for scent stimuli 🌿

If we notice correspondingly interested behaviour in our dog, we give the interest some time – but only as long as the dog does not signal an attempt to break away. After a few seconds of observing, we calmly bring our dog into the “down”, at the same time crouching down or even lying down next to him, and observe the situation as a team.
If necessary, we talk to our dog in a soothing way, but with as little emotion as possible – even rather bored – ideally with the given “down”, in order to consolidate our dog in his position.
If the source of the stimulus is of a harmless nature, we let it pass without changing our position as a team. In the best case, the source of the stimulus does not notice us.

If the source of the stimulus is to be assessed as rather problematic, we begin to move gently and calmly out of the likely approach zone – and we do so until our dog shows us through his behaviour that he is ready to take up the observation position with us again. From a safe distance, we watch the situation to the end. Once the source of the stimulus has disappeared, we praise our dog generously and continue our ramble.

Over time, we therefore train our dog to react calmly when interesting scents arrive, and we support him with the harmonising pattern of reaction we have acquired during training: observing calmly together and calmly going into the “down” with the dog.
Basics and preparation 👂
At first, we train in quiet, remote terrain without disruptive distraction. We should already have been out with the dog for a while beforehand, so that he has had some exercise.

As learned in the TEAM WALK, we move calmly through the terrain. We watch our dog attentively and notice when he stops mid-stride and listens intently with his head raised and fixed in one direction. In doing so, he pricks his ears as far as his anatomy allows. He behaves very quietly and briefly holds his breath.
Compared with humans, our dog has hearing that is up to 8 times better, which far surpasses our human hearing abilities, particularly in the high-frequency range.
Procedure for acoustic stimuli 🔇

If we notice a reaction to acoustic stimuli in our dog, we calmly slow our steps to a halt. Depending on the situation, we briefly give the dog time to take in the scene. However, before an attempt to break away or another reaction occurs, we bring the dog into the “down” and position ourselves relaxed behind our dog.
If the source of the stimulus is of a harmless nature, we let it pass without changing our position as a team. In the best case, the source of the stimulus does not notice us.

If the source of the stimulus is to be assessed as rather problematic and the attempt to bring the dog into the “down” fails, we begin to move briskly and calmly out of the approach zone – and we do so until our dog shows us through his behaviour that he is ready to take up the observation position with us again. Depending on the situation, this may involve distances of up to several dozen metres. From a safe distance, we watch the situation to the end.
Once the source of the stimulus has disappeared, we praise our dog generously and continue our ramble.

Over time, we therefore train our dog to react calmly when interesting acoustic influences arrive, and we support him with the harmonising pattern of reaction we have acquired during training: observing calmly together and calmly going into the “down” with the dog.
Important notes ⚠️
Avoid excited and restless behaviour.
Avoid moving through the terrain too quickly.
Avoid everything that strongly distracts our dog.
Practical impulse: The team observes together

The core of scouting techniques lies in perceiving together: when your dog pauses and listens or sniffs, pause as well. Become part of the observation, not its interruption. Only go into the “down” with him once you have calmly assessed the situation yourself – this shared attention is the foundation of genuine teamwork.
→ Does our dog know “down” reliably?
→ Am I already training the TEAM WALK?
→ Am I out with the dog calmly and attentively?
→ Am I completely free of distraction while out?
→ Do I communicate calmly with my dog?
→ Do I recognise my dog’s reaction patterns to external stimuli at all times and respond appropriately?
→ Am I relaxed, and do I convey this to my dog?
→ Do I bring the necessary calm at all times and observe pauses between the individual steps?
→ Do I end every exercise calmly and with praise, following the instructions?
